entries.title: The 1996-2002 telecom fiber overbuild

facts.text: The Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond reported that U.S. investment in communications equipment grew from approximately $62 billion per year in the first quarter of 1996 to over $135 billion per year in the fourth quarter of 2000, in constant 1996 dollars.

source.title: Boom and Bust in Telecommunications, Economic Quarterly Volume 89/4 (Fall 2003)

facts.text: The same article reported that communications equipment investment fell to under $93 billion in the fourth quarter of 2001, only 69 percent of the level one year earlier.

source.title: Boom and Bust in Telecommunications, Economic Quarterly Volume 89/4 (Fall 2003)

facts.text: The article stated that by early 2001 it had become apparent that massive overinvestment had taken place in the telecommunications sector, particularly in long-distance fiber-optic cable.

source.title: Boom and Bust in Telecommunications, Economic Quarterly Volume 89/4 (Fall 2003)

facts.text: The article reported that consumption of telecommunications services grew steadily from approximately $88 billion in 1995 to $151 billion in 2001, in constant 1996 dollars.

source.title: Boom and Bust in Telecommunications, Economic Quarterly Volume 89/4 (Fall 2003)

facts.text: The article reported that telecommunications industry employment peaked at approximately 1.59 million workers in March 2001 and declined 22 percent to about 1.30 million by July 2003.

source.title: Boom and Bust in Telecommunications, Economic Quarterly Volume 89/4 (Fall 2003)

facts.text: The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco reported that capital investment by publicly traded telecom service companies rose from $47 billion in 1995 to a peak of $121 billion in 2000 and fell to $49 billion by 2002.

source.title: The Boom and Bust in Information Technology Investment, FRBSF Economic Review 2004
source.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

facts.text: A Federal Reserve Board working paper stated that more than 90 percent of the optical fiber cables installed during the 1990s were left unused in the years that followed.

source.title: Learning By Investing: Embodied Technology and Business Cycles (Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2007-15)
source.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

facts.text: The same paper noted that this level of unused fiber was also partly due to a new signal transmitting technology that dramatically increased the transmitting capacity of each cable.

source.title: Learning By Investing: Embodied Technology and Business Cycles (Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2007-15)
source.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

facts.text: A 2003 academic paper from the University of Minnesota estimated that U.S. Internet traffic had approximately doubled every year since 1997, and described 1995 and 1996 as an anomalous two-year period when traffic grew at about the rate of a doubling every 100 days.

source.title: Internet traffic growth: Sources and implications

facts.text: A 2026 Federal Reserve Board staff note, using Bureau of Economic Analysis data, reported that the U.S. intellectual property and equipment investment share of GDP reached 11.5 percent in 2000 and that as of the first quarter of 2026 it was about 0.8 percentage points above its 2024 level and slightly below the 2000 peak.

source.title: Do Major Technology Advancements Lead to Overinvestment? (FEDS Notes)
source.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

entries.title: How much electricity data centres use

facts.text: A December 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated that U.S. data centers consumed 176 TWh of electricity in 2023, representing 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

source.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (LBNL-2001637)

facts.text: The Department of Energy reported that total data center electricity usage climbed from 58 TWh in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023.

source.title: DOE Releases New Report Evaluating Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers

facts.text: The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated that data center electricity use remained fairly stable at about 60 TWh between 2014 and 2016.

source.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (LBNL-2001637)

facts.text: The report states that in 2017 GPU-accelerated servers for artificial intelligence became a significant enough portion of the data center server stock that total data center electricity use began to increase again.

source.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (LBNL-2001637)

entries.title: Grid interconnection queues

facts.text: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued Order No. 2023 on July 28, 2023 to reform the procedures and agreements that transmission providers use to connect new generating facilities to the transmission system.

source.title: Explainer on the Interconnection Final Rule (Order No. 2023, Docket No. RM22-14-000)

facts.text: FERC stated that as of the end of 2022 there were over 10,000 active interconnection requests in queues throughout the United States, representing over 2,000 gigawatts of potential generation and storage capacity.

source.title: Explainer on the Interconnection Final Rule (Order No. 2023, Docket No. RM22-14-000)

facts.text: FERC stated that of the 2,179 interconnection studies completed in 2022, 68% were issued late.

source.title: Explainer on the Interconnection Final Rule (Order No. 2023, Docket No. RM22-14-000)

facts.text: Order No. 2023 requires transmission providers to replace the serial first-come, first-served study process with a first-ready, first-served cluster study process that studies proposed generating facilities in batches.

source.title: Explainer on the Interconnection Final Rule (Order No. 2023, Docket No. RM22-14-000)

facts.text: Order No. 2023 requires interconnection customers to demonstrate 90% site control when they submit an interconnection request and 100% site control when they execute the facilities study agreement.

source.title: Explainer on the Interconnection Final Rule (Order No. 2023, Docket No. RM22-14-000)

facts.text: Order No. 2023 introduced penalties for transmission providers that miss study deadlines and withdrawal penalties for interconnection customers whose withdrawal materially affects the cost or timing of other requests with an equal or lower queue position.

source.title: Explainer on the Interconnection Final Rule (Order No. 2023, Docket No. RM22-14-000)

facts.text: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory reported that as of the end of 2025 about 8,200 projects, representing 1,312 GW of generation and approximately 749 GW of storage, were actively seeking grid interconnection in the U.S.

source.title: Queued Up: 2026 Edition, Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection As of the End of 2025

facts.text: The laboratory reported that the median project built in 2025 took 61 months from interconnection request to commercial operation.

source.title: Queued Up: 2026 Edition, Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection As of the End of 2025 (report slides, PDF)

facts.text: The laboratory reported that only 13% of the capacity that submitted interconnection requests from 2000 to 2020 had reached commercial operation by the end of 2025, while 75% had been withdrawn and 10% was still active.

source.title: Queued Up: 2026 Edition, Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection As of the End of 2025

facts.text: The laboratory reported that active natural gas capacity in interconnection queues increased 86% in 2025 to 253 GW.

source.title: Queued Up: 2026 Edition, Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection As of the End of 2025

entries.title: Cooling the AI data centre

facts.text: The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory 2024 data center report defines power usage effectiveness as the total electricity demand of a data center divided by the electricity demand of its IT equipment.

source.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (LBNL-2001637)

facts.text: The report defines water usage effectiveness as the total water consumption of a data center divided by the electricity demand of its IT equipment.

source.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (LBNL-2001637)

facts.text: The report states that a waterside economizer is well suited for liquid cooling methods such as rear door heat exchangers, direct-to-chip cooling and immersion.

facts.text: The report states that liquid-cooled IT systems can often be operated at higher water or refrigerant temperatures than air-cooled IT systems.

source.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (LBNL-2001637)
